text:
The envelope arrived with a window; ours won't shut
November threads a needle through the plywood that I cut
I count the quarter mountain on a towel beside the sink
The dryer eats a dollar, so the towels acquire a stink
My daughter draws a castle on the back of Final Notice
I tell her add a drawbridge; she asks why nobody's home yet
The landlord calls me William like the lease contains my father
My boss calls me tomorrow; that's a different kind of dollar
I sold the amp on Tuesday, kept the cable for a reason
A cord without an instrument can still conduct a grieving
There's forty in the flour tin, eleven in my boot
A five behind her photograph; I hate what pictures do
I knock downstairs with half, rehearsing fractions into sentences
He looks past me at her castle, then revises when the ending is
Back upstairs, she asks if kings are rich; I say, 'Depends'
And tape the paper drawbridge where the broken window ends

At two, the office aquarium reflects my yellow gloves
Those fish have seen the partners do what partners never discuss
I scrub a crescent coffee stain beneath the chairman's chair
His framed award says Leadership; a beetle's sleeping there
The elevator clears its throat and swallows floor thirteen
I ride beside a birthday cake abandoned by the team
Pink frosting spells Congratulations, nobody left to claim it
I cut myself the corner where the plastic knife won't cave in
My cart has one rebellious wheel that squeals around the turn
I know which desk has grief because its little lamp still burns
Her husband died in August; now she folds his shirts at work
I leave that wastebasket alone; some scraps deserve the earth
At five, I polish fingerprints from glass I cannot see through
Security says morning like he's testing if it's legal
Outside, the sun starts clocking in behind the bank's gold lettering
I punch out with a piece of cake, still tasting someone's better thing

You kept your lunch inside a glove so nobody would take it
I learned to throw a punch before I learned what it was saving
Same room, two beds, your ceiling stars were peeling into mine
You'd point at missing constellations, tell me, 'That's a sign'
Now county sends your letters with the staples confiscated
Your bird has got no wings because the ink got saturated
You ask about the radiator, not about your hearing
I write, 'It knocks,' and leave out how your little boy keeps listening
He says the pipes are Daddy, coming up to fix the heat
I squat beside his sneakers, cannot get the tongues to meet
Your lawyer wants a number that my bank app won't pronounce
I sell the bike we built with seven different bikes' accounts
You call and say I'm not supposed to put my life on pause
I say the phone is breaking up; I hear you through the fraud
Tonight I patch the ceiling, leave your paper planets hanging
Your son needs somewhere bigger than this room to put his asking

Her recipe says some; no cup has ever earned her trust
She measures with the knuckle that the factory nearly crushed
A saucepan with a wobble does a shuffle on the grate
She puts a folded bill beneath the table, not beneath my plate
The radio discusses wars; she argues with the onions
Says men who never peel a thing keep telling us of suffering
I brought a fancy olive oil; she used it on the hinge
That cabinet stopped complaining; now she says the stuff's a win
The window wears a grease film like an old translucent map
I trace the route I took away; she wipes it with a rag
I used to hate the smell that rode my jacket into school
Now every spotless restaurant feels short a crucial tool
She asks if I am eating; I recite my recent bookings
She lifts the lid, says, 'That ain't what I asked,' and keeps on looking
I set my phone face down beside the chipped ceramic hen
She serves me with the good hand, then she serves me once again

They boxed my sister's summer in a room without a season
One sandal, two receipts, a photograph with no agreed-on meaning
Detective wore a different tie each time he said 'No leads'
I memorized the patterns; that's what helplessness can teach
Her poster in the laundromat went blue around the mouth
The owner moved it higher when the floodwater came south
I learned to read a river by what branches it retained
Learned everybody's theory has a person it protects from blame
This April, they assigned a woman younger than my sister
She asked about the night before; her pencil didn't whisper
I said we fought about a dress; she wrote the color down
Not victim, not a case file: yellow, bought the next town out
She called on Friday, said the dress was folded in a locker
A name was on the rental slip; she couldn't tell me proper
For once I did not promise Mom we'd have her home by June
I sat and peeled an orange, kept the peel inside the room

My auntie kept the carbon copies, blue beneath her nails
She said a mouth can change its story; paper leaves a trail
The county took our orchard for a road that never came
Now trucks haul gravel through a business with the mayor's maiden name
I spread the deeds on card tables beside the bingo cages
The church fan lifts the corner of a decade's missing pages
There's seventeen identical mistakes in separate bids
A typo more dependable than anybody's lips
The clerk who used to shoo me out starts taking lunch at one
She leaves a carton marked Disposal where the public lift gets stuck
I bring no hidden microphone, just sleeves against the dust
And find our parcel underneath a shell with zero trucks
At council, they reduce my speaking time to ninety seconds
I read the account numbers till the chairman interrupts them
A woman in the back begins to copy what I say
By Monday, every windscreen down our block has page eight

The belt makes little mountains out of boxes marked FRAGILE
I stack a toaster on a crib and call that work-life balance
My scanner chirps approval like a bird that never sleeps
Its screen subtracts the seconds that I stop to flex my knees
There's mandatory voluntary hours on the roster
The sentence has a broken bone; nobody calls a doctor
At ten, my kid sends footage of his trumpet solo, sideways
I watch it with no volume while the forklift blocks the fire lane
He lifts his eyes where I should sit; the camera dips
I send a row of clapping hands with cardboard fingertips
The supervisor offers double Sunday if I sign
I ask him double what; he taps his watch instead of mine
At home, the hallway night-light puts his silhouette on stage
He brings the trumpet half asleep, the bell a quarter raised
He plays the place he missed, then plays it clean without a stop
I do not check the time; the kitchen clock can watch

You called me Mister Allen for the first eleven months
I answered every syllable; a title ain't a grudge
Your father had a nickname for you I had never heard
It slipped out when you slept; I didn't try to steal the word
I learned your bike had backwards brakes and you disliked tomatoes
Your mother said be patient; you said, 'You can't make me say so'
The first school form I signed, I put my name outside the box
No square for what I was, just mother, father, other, crossed
At twelve, you swung at me because I wouldn't lend the keys
I caught your wrist, then let it go; you stared at what I'd freed
We sat apart all evening, letting halftime pass for peace
I fixed your jacket zipper, left the pull tab near your keys
Years later, at the hospital, the intake asked for kin
You shoved the clipboard toward me, pushed a ballpoint in my fist
I asked if you were sure; you rolled your eyes, said, 'Who else?'
I wrote inside the box this time, and kept that to myself

The driver knows the pothole by the church and eases left
His thermos has a dent exactly where the mirror's bent
I carry six unsold bouquets beneath my borrowed coat
The roses snag my lining like they want to miss their stop
A cook sits with his apron folded over both his knees
The woman at the hospital still wears her plastic sleeves
Nobody speaks; the heater has a rattling dissertation
It argues with the windows through another empty station
A kid gets on with fifty cents and counts it twice for proof
The driver waves him past; the cook shifts over, makes him room
We're all pretending not to see the kindness as it happens
As if a decent thing needs darkness more than any damage
I leave a rose beside the farebox; 'Change?' he calls me back
I tell him, 'Keep it'; first time that I've ever managed that
Behind me, red tail lights go stitching up the rain
I take the stairs two at a time; my mother stayed awake

The strap leaves little squares of summer printed on my skin
I shower with one leg outside, a flamingo in a tin
The charger cord won't reach the couch; I sleep beside the socket
My dreams have got a radius, my sweat has got a docket
At orientation, 'Any questions?' sounded like a dare
I asked if jobs beyond the bridge could count; she said, 'Depends where'
The map cut through the loading dock where all new hires clock in
My boss said use the other door; the fence said try again
My niece calls it a robot pet and asks what it can eat
I tell her electricity; she sets a grape beside my feet
Some nights the signal drops and turns the doorway into weather
I call before they call me, reading case and serial letters
The morning they remove it, I expect a kind of flight
Instead my sock sits crooked where the skin forgot the light
I cross the bridge on foot and buy a coffee past the tracks
The cup is hot; I stand there till my body trusts that fact

The check arrived with my name right, an unfamiliar pleasure
I'd spent a week called New Kid, hauling doors in burning weather
The foreman said don't lose it; I could hear the joke approach
I folded it inside the bus pass that I'd borrowed from my folks
The check place took a corner; said convenience has a fee
I watched the woman count the hours she was peeling off of me
Bought insoles first, the kind with gel the color of a glacier
Then paid the man who let me slide on last month's radiator
A chicken, rice, a birthday card three weeks beyond the date
A comb with all its teeth; I made the woman at the checkout wait
I used to pull a broken one through hair and call it fine
Now here was this ridiculous small luxury of mine
I gave my mother cash; she tucked it back inside my palm
I put it in the light bill, slid the envelope along
She flicked the kitchen switch twice, made a little theater
That night the dark was optional; we chose it for the meter

The vending spiral holds my crackers hostage in its teeth
I thump the glass, then stop; there's enough alarms beneath
My father's slippers face each other under chair eighteen
I brought them in a grocery bag; he hates to show his feet
A resident says numbers like they're places we could visit
I nod as if my father is a country with statistics
My sister does the talking; I maintain the phone at charge
We find our little jobs when all the useful ones are barred
The cleaner lifts our sneaker soles to mop beneath the waiting
We rise, apologize, then sit, the polished floor still shaking
Dad wakes at four and asks if someone fed the orange cat
There isn't any orange cat; I tell him I'll handle that
He grips my sleeve, says don't let him scratch the leather chair
His fingers close so fiercely on a thing that isn't there
At dawn my sister finds me, saucer balanced by the door
Calling to an orange shape I haven't seen before

He tests my mother's sewing pedal with a boot too big
The needle dips through nothing; still, I hear the prom dress stitch
He says, 'Domestic model,' like that makes it less a machine
It paid for two extractions and a season of Little League
I lay the manual beside it, every margin in her cursive
He slides it back; the pencil marks don't count toward the purchase
Behind him, twenty wedding bands sit sorted out by weight
No shelf for what they promised, just the metal and the grade
I need the tire fixed by Monday, need the Monday route
He offers eighty; I say ninety, leave her labor out
The ticket has a date by which the past becomes his stock
I fold it in the manual and walk around the block
Three Fridays later, I return with grease beneath my nails
He brings it out already threaded, ready for a sale
At home I press the pedal, make a seam that leans to port
Then pull the crooked thread and try again on my work shorts

The architect said transparency; my wife called it exposure
We learned the neighbors' dinners from the light across the clover
Our dishes matched the catalog, our fights did not photograph
We whispered by the boiler where the windows couldn't catch
I taught the boys to wave before I taught them how to knock
The little one asked why our rooms looked like a jewelry box
At parties, I performed a marriage, cufflinks bright as ice
She stood beside the orchids, pinching roots to check for life
The hail came down in August, hard as thrown aquarium stones
We sheltered in the pantry with the flour and the phones
A pane above the dining table cracked from edge to center
Nobody moved to film it; that's the part that I remember
Next morning, I called three men out to price a wooden wall
She asked if I was hiding us; I said, 'Not us. Not all'
We kept one window facing where the pear tree drops its fruit
And hung the boys' bad paintings in the room we couldn't shoot

A dashboard says my character is five hundred and eight
It doesn't show the ambulance, just who was thirty days late
The sofa salesman changes to a smaller kind of smile
His weekly plan would outlive every spring beneath that pile
I calculate the interest on the back of his brochure
Three couches for one couch; he says the payments are secure
My father used to hide the mail beneath the brown recliner
I thought the chair was heavy; now I know what lived inside it
At home, my son and I build seating out of shipping crates
He sands the splintered edges, asks what makes a number change
I say it's what they trust us with; he says, 'They don't know you'
A person should get old before a sentence cuts that true
I set the smallest bill to clear before the late fee lands
The graph creeps up a pixel; I unclench my empty hands
He paints our wooden couch bright green, then writes his name below
Nobody can repossess the afternoon it took us both

The organ has a wheezing key we work around in F
Miss Vera folds her coat beneath the pew where her man slept
The pastor's son is missing; still, the pastor leads the prayer
His collar sits a little loose, a finger's width of air
I came because my mother asked; my boots defile the tile
With half the mud the building site had gathered in a mile
The sermon turns to giving; I prepare my usual exit
Then Reverend says the furnace broke, and names the actual estimate
No kingdom on a payment plan, just cold in the back room
Where every Tuesday women bring the kids who need the food
I raise my hand; not testimony, just a heating license
He blinks and asks me afterward; I tell him, 'Let's go find it'
We miss the benediction checking breakers in the basement
He holds the flashlight steady while I trace the ventilation
Upstairs, they start the final hymn; warm air comes through the grate
I don't know what I believe; I know what I repaired today

Mr. Han can spot a fake ten from the sound against the till
But takes my uncle's handwritten IOUs against his will
His daughter labels everything in two competing scripts
I learned to spell persimmon where the lottery tickets sit
The freezer has a tremor like a bass note through a wall
We slap its side in passing; that's our maintenance protocol
One shelf has been on clearance since the year my sister married
Those candles watched her wedding, watched the split and all the baggage
A chain has bought the building; there's a notice by the scales
He says they want a wine bar, says it like a foreign ailment
We plan a noisy protest; he asks who will buy the stock
So Saturday we empty shelves and sweep behind the mop
He tears the little credit book in strips above the bin
My uncle tries to pay; he says, 'You bring the chairs back in'
The final bell rings crooked when he pulls the door to lock
We take the chairs across the street and sit there with the block

My phone still thinks you're available at seven simple taps
It offers me your contact when I type the word 'perhaps'
Your birthday gets a candle; it can wish you well on cue
This thing can route me through a storm but can't stop routing me to you
I rang your number once and heard a woman say hello
A television laughed behind her; I forgot the word for no
I said I'd got the wrong one, which was true enough to hurt
Then saved her under Do Not Call, absurd administrative work
There's Mom's old landline, disconnected after we sold
The house with the extension cord that never reached the stove
My thumb can find those digits without asking me for help
A tiny muscle keeping what the companies have shelved
Tonight I write the numbers in a book beside the bed
Not so that I can reach you; so I know where they are kept
I clear a little space; the phone suggests a brighter screen
I let it darken, hear the fridge, and leave a page between

You asked for Saturn on the cake, not princesses or glitter
The baker made an orange with a ring that looked like dinner
I nearly asked him change it, then you said, 'That's Titan, Dad'
And drew a moon in frosting with the fork you'd smuggled back
Your mother sent the candles; we exchanged them at the curb
Two people being careful with the sharp end of a word
I booked the bowling alley, couldn't fill the second lane
Your friends wore socks with planets; you instructed me on names
I rolled a gutter ball; you called it gravitational drift
Then put the bumpers up for me, a quiet little gift
At home you opened presents, put the paper on a mat
Kept every sheet for roofing on your cardboard landing pad
I thought a birthday needed more than what my checkbook lost
You asked if we could stay up till the station crossed the roof
We watched one moving pinprick, shared the blanket on the grass
You whispered, 'People live in that,' your bare feet on my calf

I learned the house by listening before I learned the street
Which stair complained, which cupboard meant somebody hadn't eaten
They gave me room to put my things; my things remained a bag
A drawer can look like ownership; I wasn't fooled by that
Mrs. Bell would knock, then wait until I said come in
The waiting was the strange part, not the tapping, not the grin
She asked what I liked eating; I said anything was cool
Then hid a roll inside a sock before I left for school
She found it in the laundry, placed a breadbox on my shelf
No meeting in the kitchen, no discussion of my health
In March, I broke her blue bowl; every fragment had an ear
I packed the bag, rehearsed the part where I would disappear
She swept it up, said, 'Hated it,' then cried, 'My sister made it'
I stayed to hold the dustpan, learning two things could be stated
That night I put my shirts away, one drawer, not all at once
And kept the bag beneath the bed; she never made me budge

My alarm is three tin spoons inside a cracked blue cup
I keep it past the mattress so my whole self must get up
The bakery back entrance has a lock that hates the frost
I warm the key between my palms and calculate the cost
Of sleeping twenty minutes more, of missing twenty rolls
Of flour in the lungs that make the singing on the stroll
The dough has risen overnight without a supervisor
I punch it down, apologize; we're different kinds of tired
At six, the rich man's driver buys a twist for his employer
At seven, buys one for himself and eats behind the boiler
We split the batch that browned too far; the bitter edge is sweet
He says the kid is walking now, shows video on repeat
Tomorrow will repeat the key, the dough, the early dark
But I put two bent rolls aside and mark his name in chalk
When he comes in, I ask which way the little one can turn
He holds his hands an inch apart; I stop to watch and learn

The lot was never empty; that's the first thing on the form
A fox had raised a family beneath the billboard torn
Across a painted swimming pool and valet parking sign
We called it Lake Whatever when the drains declined to drain
My cousin learned to reverse there, between a tire and chair
Miss June grew mint in buckets no one had the nerve to share
A survey crew put ribbons where the shortstop used to stand
We asked them who had bought it; they said, 'Check the county plans'
The meeting showed a meadow with a jogging silhouette
No fox, no mint, no cousins, not a scrap of what's been kept
I brought a photograph of kids reflected in the flood
The planner said it wasn't safe; I said, 'Then work with us'
We won a strip along the fence, not victory, but ground
Enough to plant the mint and keep a path that circles round
The fox moved on before the diggers took the billboard down
We left a gap beneath the fence, not knowing if it counts

I park behind the urgent care, beneath the busted P
The engine ticks a little sermon back at me in heat
Inside, they're fitting hearing aids my brother won't admit
He needs; he says the world should learn to talk and get to it
I used to pray with offers, draw a ledger, title: Goodness
Three sober weeks should buy me one encouraging conclusion
But nothing on the dashboard takes a payment or a vow
The plastic saint has melted, leaning permanently south
A woman in the next car eats an apple with a knife
She sees the tea I've spilled and passes towels to my side
No question, no conversion, just a square of folded white
I wipe my hands and let the motor rest a little while
My brother steps outside; a bird is scraping through the trees
He stops beneath the branch, looks up, and points it out to me
I ask what it is saying; he says, 'How the hell should I know?'
We stand there hearing something neither one of us can own

Derek loves a crisis when the camera has a charge
He posted Free My Brother; couldn't tell you which court ours
He sent a flame emoji when the kitchen caught a flame
Then asked if we could tag his page in posts about the claim
Meanwhile, quiet Leon has a van that smells like grout
He came at six with bins and didn't ask what this was 'bout
We salvaged three wet albums, half a kettle, all the spoons
He laid my mother's pictures face-up in his spare room
Derek booked a fundraiser, described himself as chair
The restaurant comped dinner; somehow we were never there
I send the smoke-removal bill; he asks to be untagged
Funny how the helping hands get busy with their bags
He says I've changed; I have, I count support in hours supplied
A scraper on the blistered paint, not hearts beneath a crying sign
When Leon's van quit running, I was underneath by nine
We passed the wrench in silence; both our phones stayed up inside

I change my shirt in transit where the tunnel blacks the glass
From pharmacy maroon to diner blue, seven seconds flat
The first name tag has left a dent the second can't conceal
By Friday, call out Coffee; I respond before I feel
At job one, I shelve remedies for people who can't sleep
At job two, I pour the reason that their remedies run weak
The register at either place won't take my bus receipt
I spend an hour between them; neither buys that hour from me
My girlfriend leaves me supper, 'Please don't microwave the greens'
Then, smaller, 'We should talk when you're not falling half asleep'
I read it on a Tuesday, which is technically my Sunday
My second shoe stays on all night; I never get it unlaced
Next week I trade a shift and take a sandwich to her lunch
We sit beside the dumpsters; she tells stories, I don't rush
The truck comes, drowns her punchline; we both wait for it to leave
She starts again from somewhere she saved specially for me

The plastic on the sofa makes a thunderclap in shorts
Grandma says it's preservation; I say furniture needs pores
Her biscuits come in butter tins, the butter tin holds thread
The actual butter's in a bowl a dead aunt painted red
She knows the neighbor's business from the angle of their blinds
And calls the weather foolish when it disagrees with her spine
We try to buy her something new; she asks what broke on this
Then fixes our expensive things with pliers and a pin
The last time I came over, there were labels on the doors
In handwriting I recognized but hadn't seen before
She asked if I was hungry three times in half an hour
I said yes every time; we made a mountain out of flour
Her hands remembered biscuits when my name would not come through
I watched them turn the mixture, asked her how much milk to use
She laughed and said, 'You'll feel it,' pressed my fingers in the bowl
I keep that recipe in places paper doesn't go

The tailor asks which shoulder drops; I say the one with weight
He smiles before he sees the black, then puts the chalk away
This suit was for a wedding when my brother wore it first
He spilled a little gravy where the lining meets the shirt
I'm wider now; the trousers hold their breath around my thighs
He lets them out an inch; we practice standing without lies
At service, everybody wants a piece of how he sounded
I give them all the good jokes, keep the cruel one that I counted
The night he called me useless, then returned to fix my brakes
I loved him, not a version with his rough parts rubbed away
His daughter grabs the jacket, wipes her nose against the sleeve
Her mother reaches for her; I say, 'Please just let it be'
Outside, a pigeon picks a chip from underneath the hearse
Life has such appalling manners; I nearly laugh, then burst
At home I hang the jacket; now the wedding smells like rain
The left sleeve's stiff; I cannot bring myself to clean the stain

The ceiling crack starts over by the curtain, branches twice
I've named its longest tributary Things I Should've Tried
The fridge kicks on; a motorcycle stitches through the quiet
My mind convenes a hearing where the witness can't deny it
Exhibit A: the email with 'unfortunately' centered
Exhibit B: a laugh I heard in school and still remember
The prosecution brings a chair; it's planning quite a stay
I turn the pillow over, grant a motion for delay
My therapist said notice without building it a room
I notice that I'm building it; the room gets a room too
At three fifteen, I put both feet on carpet, count the fibers
Name five unimportant objects, one of them a spider
It works the ceiling corner, briefly hangs by its own hair
I do not need its lesson, just another body there
I fetch a cup, then leave it; neither one of us must go
The crack becomes a crack again; the window starts to show

The doorway has my height in pencil, six to seventeen
I take a picture straight-on, put a ruler in the scene
My mother says the new folks will repaint it anyway
Then rubs her thumb beside the marks and walks the other way
The couch won't make the corner; we contend with screw and board
And curse the younger versions of ourselves who forced it through before
Behind the missing cushion: coins, a tooth, a cinema stub
A fossil bed of evenings when the whole of us was us
My room sounds bigger empty; I don't care for the acoustics
I whisper just to check if there's a way the house can lose me
We label boxes fragile that have never held much glass
Her mixer, my diplomas, all the photographs of Dad
The landlord comes at four; she hands the keys over in pairs
Then checks her purse for something that she knows is no more there
I drive us to her smaller place, put kettle on the stove
She asks me where the cups are; I say, 'Tell me where they go'

They want the opening empty, just a boy without a thing
But Mom had bought the notebook, and the church had let me sing
Mr. Flores lent a drill, said bring the batteries back
A bus mechanic waived a fare when rain destroyed my cash
My sister gave me Sundays that she could have used for sleeping
She watched my kid while I recorded underneath a leaking ceiling
I had a cousin's old computer, crooked keys and noisy fan
A teacher kept the music room unlocked against the plan
So no, I didn't conjure all this timber out of ether
The platform had a dozen hands beneath it like a creature
I built with what they gave me, sometimes badly, sometimes late
Still owe a man a ladder; still owe several folks a day
The interviewer asks how I surpassed the rest
I ask him leave that question in, then start to list addresses
Not where they live, the places they made room for me to start
Put those inside the credits; let the credits be the bars
